title: Midnight burst GPU pool throttling - handoff notes
content:
TL;DR:

Between 2026-03-04 23:40 UTC and 2026-03-05 01:15 UTC we observed repeated transient throughput drops across a subset of the Dedicated GPU pool (cluster: ded-gpu-eu-2). Symptoms looked like a short-lived but high-volume burst of long-running model sessions consuming KV cache and holding GPUs for >10x expected token-time. Autoscaler reacted by trimming pods, which triggered credential eviction race vs. workload failover and further reduced capacity; customers using reserved slots saw increased p99 latency and throughput loss. Immediate mitigations restored user-facing capacity at 00:45 UTC but a full stable state required manual pod pinning and a short maintenance window.

What this doc is: handoff + initial incident review + runbook draft of actions we needed but didn’t have codified. Not a final blameless postmortem; this captures observations, hypotheses, evidence, commands, and concrete follow-ups for the next 72h.

Timeline (UTC):
- 2026-03-04 23:38 - Pager fired: Dedicated GPU pool p99 latency spike (alert rule: ded-gpu-p99-latency > 1.2s for 3m)
- 23:40 - Oncall (Riley) joins Slack alert channel, checks console (Console -> Dedicated -> ded-gpu-eu-2).
- 23:43 - Metrics: per-host GPU utilization high (95%), active long sessions (avg duration 210s vs baseline 18s). Token emission rate per-session dropped, backlog increased.
- 23:47 - Observed simultaneous queue growth on prefix cache eviction metrics (cache_evictions/s spiked).
- 23:55 - Autoscaler attempt: scale-down events triggered by controller (scale-down grace RT < configured min-up-time). Several pods terminated while holding KV shards. Pod churn led to increased tail latencies as clients reattached.
- 00:05 - Applied temporary mitigation: disable aggressive scale-down on ded-gpu-eu-2 (kubectl annotate nodegroup autoscale=disabled @ eu-2 for 20m).
- 00:18 - Manual intervention: pin 6 healthy pods to reserve capacity for canary flows (label set: reserved-oncall=true).
- 00:30 - Observed KPIs improving; by 00:45 observed p99 back to normal and eviction rate decreased.
- 01:15 - Declared incident under control.

Key signals and evidence:
- session_duration_histogram mean jumped from 18s -> 205s (sources: runtime/latency, model-profiles).
- cache_evictions/s correlated strongly with p99 latency (cross-corr coefficient ~0.82 over incident window).
- Autoscaler logs: several scale-downs initiated because nodegroup utilization measure reported short-term drop (metrics pipeline noise due to metric aggregates being computed on incomplete windows).
- Pod termination logs show preStop hooks completed but KV persistence hand-off sometimes timed out (timeouts at ~10s).

Primary hypothesis (most likely chain):
A) A workload (unknown customer flow) caused a burst of long-running requests that monopolized KV cache and pinned GPU memory. B) The autoscaler, interpreting short-term utilization patterns, initiated scale-downs at the same time, evicting pods that still owned KV cache shards. C) Evictions forced client reconnects and KV rehydrations which increased load and created a feedback loop, prolonging session durations and raising p99 latency.

Secondary hypotheses to validate (lower confidence):
- A sub-version of a model with different KV-churn characteristics was rolled into the cluster the same evening (check model deployment events).
- A monitoring aggregator bug underreported in-flight tokens causing autoscaler to underestimate real utilization for brief windows.

Immediate mitigations we executed (and why):
- Disabled aggressive scaler for ded-gpu-eu-2 for 20 minutes to prevent further eviction-triggered cascades. Rationale: allow current sessions to drain naturally and avoid repeated handoffs.
- Pinned reserve pods with label reserved-oncall=true to guarantee minimal capacity for critical traffic. Rationale: quick buffer while we diagnose.
- Raised sync-level logging on kv-manager for 30m to capture shard handoff traces. Rationale: need detailed evidence of handoff timeouts.

What worked:
- Pinning reserve pods restored enough capacity to stop the feedback loop quickly.
- Disabling scale-down prevented further evictions and allowed smoother drain.

What failed / runbook gaps uncovered:
- No explicit runbook step for 'scale-down vs KV-ownership' race; current runbooks assume pods free memory instantly on SIGTERM.
- Autoscaler sensitivity thresholds allow short-window utilization dips to trigger scale-down in high-KV churn workloads. No per-cluster overrides documented.
- Lack of a quick script to identify top active sessions by KV-shard and abort non-critical longest-run sessions safely.

Immediate follow-up actions (72h):
- (Owner: Joon) INFRA-1927: Add autoscaler policy flag 'kv-safe-minimum' to nodegroup config and expose it in console for Dedicated clusters. Due: 2026-03-12.
- (Owner: Maya) infra: Create a short script (tools/abort-long-sessions.sh) that lists sessions > 2x median and can gracefully cancel low-priority ones. Add to oncall toolbox. Due: 2026-03-11.
- (Owner: Riley) runbook: Draft dedicated-capacity-kv-eviction-playbook.md with step-by-step 'disable scale-down', 'pin reserve pods', 'how to inspect kv-manager traces' + example kubectl commands. Due: 2026-03-09.
- (Owner: Zara) monitoring: Add metric for kv_shard_handoff_time p95 and an alert when p95 > 5s. Tune alert to target pre-incident noise tolerance. Due: 2026-03-10.

Longer term (quarter roadmap):
- Autoscaler improvements: integrate a KV-ownership signal into the autoscaler to avoid evicting pods that own hot shards, plus smoothing windows for dedicated pools. (Product + Infra)
- Model deployment gating: require model onboarding to include KV-usage profile; if KV-churn is high, auto-pin minimal replica set. (Applied-ML + Serving Runtime)
- Add a 'reserved capacity' toggle in Console to temporarily raise min replicas for a cluster on demand. (Product)

Commands and snippets used during incident (for reproducibility):
- Check pods with long runtime: kubectl get pods -n inference --sort-by=.status.startTime -o wide | grep -E 'ded-gpu-eu-2'
- Disable scale-down (temporary annotation): kubectl annotate nodegroup ded-gpu-eu-2 autoscale=disabled --overwrite
- Label pins: kubectl label pod <pod-name> reserved-oncall=true
- tail kv-manager logs: kubectl logs -n infra kv-manager-0 -c kv-manager --since=60m | grep "handoff"

Open questions (to be answered in follow-ups):
- Which customer flow caused the initial burst? (Product/Customer Success to correlate request ids)
- Was there a model rollout that changed KV profile at ~23:25 UTC? (Check model-catalog events)
- Can the metric aggregation window be widened for ded clusters to avoid autoscaler noise?

Handoff to next oncall:
- If you see p99 spike for ded-gpu-eu-2 again, first check kv_shard_handoff_time p95. If it's > 5s, annotate nodegroup to disable scale-down and pin 4 pods as reserved.
- Use abort-long-sessions.sh to trim non-critical long sessions while preserving VIP/reserved flows.
- Post any action to #sre-oncall with timestamps, nodegroup annotated, and PR reference if changes made.

Notes to self / sticky points:
- Avoid immediate cluster-wide scale-down toggles unless we have clear ownership of long-running sessions; prefer targeted nodegroup-level flags.
- Try to capture one full handoff trace next incident — we currently missed the exact preStop timeout event in a couple of pods.

Appendix: metrics snapshots and quick links (copied from incident chat):
- grafana: /d/dedicated/cluster-ded-gpu-eu-2?from=1678000000000&to=1678007200000
- raw autoscaler logs (s3): s3://infra-logs/autoscaler/ded-gpu-eu-2/2026-03-04.log

End of notes.

(If you pick this up: add your own notes inline under 'Handoff to next oncall' and create a follow-up ticket for anything you take on.)
